rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Khidr acted through mystic insight into reality behind appearances, as a conscious part of God's plan; this explains the plural in 18:80–81 and attribution of the act to God's will.
rows.anchor: the mystic insight which revealed to him the reality behind the outward appearance of things and made him a conscious particle in God's unfathomable plan

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The promised account is a memorable mention because the ensuing story is a parable confined to fundamental spiritual truths.
rows.anchor: allusion to the parabolic character of the subsequent story

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Qarn can mean horn, generation, epoch, age, or century; elsewhere in the Qur'an, qarn and qurun consistently mean a generation or civilization.
rows.anchor: the noun qarn has the meaning of "horn" as well as of "generation" or "epoch" or "age" or "century"

rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: Classical commentators take Dhu'l-Qarnayn as "the Two-Horned One," apparently influenced by ancient Middle Eastern horns as symbols of power, though Asad says the Qur'an offers no warrant.
rows.anchor: The classical commentators incline to the first of these meanings ("the Two-Horned")

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad notes that every other Qur'anic use of qarn or qurun means people of a particular generation or civilization.
rows.anchor: each time it has the meaning of "generation" in the sense of people belonging to one particular epoch or civilization

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The two horns may echo familiar ancient symbolism and represent Dhu'l-Qarnayn's paired worldly royal power and spiritual strength from faith.
rows.anchor: the "two horns" may be taken to denote the two sources of power with which Dhu'l-Qarnayn is said to have been endowed

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad rejects identifying Dhu'l-Qarnayn with Alexander or pre-Islamic Himyaritic kings because they were pagans, whereas the Qur'anic figure believes in one God.
rows.anchor: makes it impossible to identify Dhu 'l-Qarnayn, as most of the commentators do, with Alexander the Great

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The story is neither history nor legend; it is a parable about faith, ethics, and the problem of worldly power.
rows.anchor: its sole purport is a parabolic discourse on faith and ethics, with specific reference to the problem of worldly power

rows.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and Ad-Dahhak
rows.claim: These authorities, as quoted by Ibn Kathir, understand sabab here as knowledge of the right means to achieve a particular end.
rows.anchor: According to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and Ad-Dahhak

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Dhu'l-Qarnayn never used wrong means, even to achieve a righteous goal.
rows.anchor: he never employed wrong means to achieve even a righteous goal

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: The setting of the sun refers to the westernmost point of Dhu'l-Qarnayn's expedition.
rows.anchor: the westernmost point of his expedition (Razi)

rows.speaker: many philologists
rows.claim: The word 'ayn, primarily meaning spring, can also mean an abundance of water.
rows.anchor: according to many philologists (cf. Taj al-'Arus), is one of the meanings of 'ayn

rows.speaker: Razi and Ibn Kathir
rows.claim: They explain the sun's apparent setting in the sea as a metaphor based on the familiar optical illusion of the sun disappearing into the sea.
rows.anchor: both of whom point out that we have here a metaphor based on the common optical illusion

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi explains the optical illusion by the earth's spherical shape and says Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i had already advanced this view in a now-lost commentary.
rows.anchor: Razi explains this, correctly, by the fact that the earth is spherical

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The permission to choose punishment or kindness expresses human free will and establishes istihsan: rulers may choose what best serves the community's maslahah, the parable's first lesson.
rows.anchor: establishes also the important legal principle of istihsan (social or moral preference) open to a ruler or government

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to compare this discussion of wrongdoing with 11:117 and its corresponding note.
rows.anchor: Cf. 11:117 and the corresponding note 149.

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The punishment described is in the hereafter, whose realities cannot be imagined or defined through human experience.
rows.anchor: nothing that pertains to the life to come could ever be imagined or defined in terms of human experience

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Because righteous conduct is the norm expected of people, its laws should not be overly demanding; this is another lesson of the parable.
rows.anchor: the laws relating thereto must not be too demanding - which is another lesson to be drawn from this parable

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: For his rendering of thumma here, Asad refers readers to his note 31 on surah 6.
rows.anchor: For this rendering of the particle thumma, see surah 6, note 31.

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The rising of the sun marks the easternmost point of the expedition, parallel to the phrase about its setting in verse 86.
rows.anchor: the easternmost point of his expedition (similar to the expression "the setting of the sun" in verse 86)

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi reads kadhalika as describing the people's primitive natural state; Dhu'l-Qarnayn left them as he found them to avoid upsetting their way of life and causing misery.
rows.anchor: This is Razi's interpretation of the isolated expression kadhalika ("thus" or "thus it was") occurring here

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The literal phrase means all that was with Dhu'l-Qarnayn, including his resolve not to corrupt God's creation; Asad calls this another ethical lesson of the parable.
rows.anchor: his resolve not to "corrupt [or "change"] God's creation" (cf. the second half

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: The location between the two mountain barriers is generally assumed to be the Caucasus.
rows.anchor: This is generally assumed to be the Caucasus.

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad dismisses location theories as irrelevant speculation because neither the Qur'an nor an authentic Tradition identifies the barriers or their people; the parable instead illustrates ethical principles.
rows.anchor: we can safely dismiss all the speculations advanced by the commentators on this score as irrelevant

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The European-language forms Gog and Magog derive from vague biblical references to Yajuj and Majuj.
rows.anchor: the basis of certain vague references to them in the Bible (Genesis x, 2, I Chronicles i, 5, Ezekiel xxxviii, 2

rows.speaker: post-classical commentators
rows.claim: Most post-classical commentators identify Gog and Magog with the Mongols and Tatars.
rows.anchor: Most of the post-classical commentators identify these tribes with the Mongols and Tatars

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: The usual interpretation takes God's establishment of Dhu'l-Qarnayn to mean the power and wealth bestowed on him.
rows.anchor: It is generally assumed that the phrase "that wherein my Sustainer has so securely established me (makkanni)" refers to the power and wealth

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad instead understands the phrase as God's guidance, which better fits the parable's ethical tenor than worldly possessions.
rows.anchor: it refers to God's guidance rather than to worldly possessions

rows.speaker: classical commentators (e.g., Tabari)
rows.claim: Some classical commentators treat the barrier's eventual breach as a definite historical event: Gog and Magog, identified as Mongols and Tatars, breaking through.
rows.anchor: Some of the classical commentators (e.g., Tabari) regard this as a prediction of a definite, historic event

rows.speaker: the Apostle of God
rows.claim: A well-authenticated report in Ibn Hanbal, Bukhari, and Muslim recounts the Prophet's dream of a small breach in Gog and Magog's barrier and his alarm for the Arabs.
rows.anchor: recorded by Ibn Hanbal, Bukhari and Muslim - which tells us that the Apostle of God had a prophetic dream

rows.speaker: Muslims since the late Middle Ages
rows.claim: Later Muslims read the dream as predicting the thirteenth-century Mongol invasion that destroyed the Abbasid Empire and Arab political power.
rows.anchor: Muslims have been inclined to discern in this dream a prediction of the great Mongol invasion in the thirteenth century

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Because verses 99–101 connect Gog and Magog with Judgment Day, Asad reads the appointed time as the Last Hour, when human works will be destroyed.
rows.anchor: the mention, in verses 99-101 of this surah, of "the Day" - i.e., the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Since the Last Hour's nearness is not measured in human time, Asad allows the historical breach and the Last Hour reading to coexist, with the breach a sign of its approach.
rows.anchor: it is possible to accept both of the above interpretations as equally valid

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad concludes, especially from 21:96–97, that Yajuj and Majuj are allegorical forces of social catastrophe, not particular tribes or beings, destroying civilization before the Last Hour.
rows.anchor: the terms Yajuj and Majuj are purely allegorical, applying not to any specific tribes or beings but to a series of social catastrophes

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The day in this verse is the Day of Judgment referred to in the preceding verse.
rows.anchor: on the Day of Judgment alluded to in the preceding verse

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The warning covers worship of created beings and natural forces, and the popular belief that living or dead saints can intercede for someone God has rejected.
rows.anchor: the worship of created beings or forces of nature, but also to the popular belief that saints, whether alive or dead

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The denial at issue is denial of God's oneness and uniqueness; no created being can influence His judgment.
rows.anchor: of God's oneness and uniqueness, and hence of the fact that no created being can have any "influence" on God's judgment

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Following Zamakhshari, Asad takes al-bahr generically to include all existing seas and renders the sea's like as "sea upon sea".
rows.anchor: the term al-bahr ("the sea") is used here in a generic sense, comprising all the seas that exist

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The Gospel account, which Asad says the Qur'an does not contradict, identifies Zachariah's wife Elisabeth as Mary's cousin.
rows.anchor: According to the account in the Gospels, not contradicted by the Qur'an, Zachariah's wife Elisabeth was a cousin of Mary

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad renders Zechariah's phrase as saying that he had never been unfortunate in his prayer to God.
rows.anchor: never have I been unfortunate in my prayer to Thee

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi says Zechariah feared his priestly kin would be too morally weak to discharge their duties with dignity and perhaps to protect Mary, whose guardian he was.
rows.anchor: would be morally too weak to fulfil theeir duties with dignity and conviction (Razi)

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Yahya means "he shall live": John will be spiritually alive and remembered forever.
rows.anchor: The name Yahya (John) signifies "he shall live", i.e., he will be spiritually alive and will be remembered forever

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: God's choice of the name was a singular distinction and a divine promise, as discussed in the note on 3:39.
rows.anchor: the fact that God Himself had chosen this name for him was a singular distinction, equivalent to a divine promise

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: God's power to originate a new chain of causes and effects prefaces the similar announcement of Jesus's birth later in this surah.
rows.anchor: This stress on God's unlimited power to bring into being a new chain of causes and effects forms here

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad refers to 3:41 and its corresponding note 29 for this sign.
rows.anchor: See 3:41 and the corresponding note 29.

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: The sequence implies John had grown old enough to receive and understand God's command.
rows.anchor: the sequence presupposes that John had in the meantime reached an age which enabled him to receive and understand God's commandment

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The compassion bestowed on John is a special gift from God.
rows.anchor: "compassion from Us" - i.e., as a special divine gift

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: John's story precedes Jesus's because John prepared the way as his precursor and because the birth announcements closely parallel one another in this surah and Al 'Imran.
rows.anchor: because John (called "the Baptist" in the Bible) was to be a precursor of Jesus, and, secondly, because of the obvious parallelism

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Mary apparently withdrew to pray and meditate undisturbed.
rows.anchor: in order to devote herself undisturbed to prayer and meditation

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathir
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir suggests the eastern place may have been a Temple chamber where Mary's mother had dedicated her to service.
rows.anchor: as Ibn Kathir suggests, signify an eastern chamber of the Temple, to the service of which Mary had been dedicated by her mother

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Ruh often means divine inspiration, but can also denote the angel or spiritual medium through which inspiration reaches God's elect; here it refers to the angel of revelation.
rows.anchor: the term ruh often denotes "divine inspiration". Occasionally, however, it is used to describe the medium through which such inspiration is imparted

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Because mortals cannot see an angel in its true form, God made the angel appear to Mary as a well-made human being.
rows.anchor: mortals cannot perceive an angel in his true manifestation, God caused him to appear to Mary "in the shape of a well-made human being"

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi understands the angel's designation as ruh to indicate that angels are purely spiritual beings without a physical element.
rows.anchor: the designation of the angel as ruh ("spirit" or "soul") indicates that this category of beings is purely spiritual, without any physical element
